Visualizing networks with cograph

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/visualizing-with-cograph.Rmd
visualizing-with-cograph.Rmd

How should a network figure be drawn so that its visual structure supports, rather than distorts, interpretation? In a Gaussian graphical model, variables are displayed as nodes and edges depict associations between pairs of variables conditional on the others. This representation helps researchers examine interdependence among psychological constructs instead of considering each construct separately (Saqr et al., 2024). Choices about network visualisation are therefore part of analysis and interpretation, not merely presentation. R tools such as qgraph have made network figures accessible (Epskamp et al., 2012), while practical guidance highlights the ways in which visual decisions can affect the conclusions readers draw (Jones et al., 2018).

A network diagram can help researchers identify groups of closely related constructs, connections between groups and negative associations. However, node positions depend on the layout algorithm, edge widths can obscure important differences in magnitude, and colours may be difficult to distinguish. Moreover, a visually prominent connection is not necessarily precisely estimated or evidence of a causal relationship. Good reporting therefore requires figures that communicate edge signs and magnitudes clearly, alongside numerical estimates, uncertainty assessments and an account of the choices used to construct the display (Burger et al., 2023).

In education, psychological networks have been used to investigate how learning-related processes operate together. Malmberg et al. (2022) used network approaches to examine the interplay between monitoring events in regulated learning, while Saqr et al. (2021) studied the relational and temporal dynamics of self-regulation in academic writing. Such applications illustrate why a network view can be useful when motivation, cognition and regulation are intertwined. They also make comparability important: a change in the apparent arrangement of nodes across figures should not be mistaken for a substantive difference between learners, groups or occasions.

This article uses cograph to visualise a Gaussian graphical model of five self-regulated learning constructs derived from model-generated survey responses (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). It moves from the default display to choices relevant to publication: node layouts and appearance, the encoding and filtering of edges, edge-weight distributions, bootstrap diagnostics, themes, comparisons between groups and figure export. Throughout, the aim is to make the relationship between the figure and the estimated network clear. The plotting chunks run only when cograph is installed.

library(psychnets)

Data

SRL_GPT contains 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, expressed as construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7. These are responses generated by a large language model (GPT), rather than observations from students, in a study of how language models respond to psychological questionnaires (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). SRL_Claude contains a further 300 model-generated responses and is used for the group comparison. The example demonstrates visualisation methods, not findings about a population of learners.

  • Nodes: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety).
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.

ebic_glasso() estimates a regularised Gaussian graphical model. Its edges represent partial correlations, with the extended Bayesian information criterion used to select the network.

fit <- ebic_glasso(SRL_GPT)
fit
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 10   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.00861   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.21e-10

The fitted network contains 10 edges. Nine are positive, with weights from 0.049 to 0.412, and the association between self-regulation and test anxiety is negative (-0.350). These values describe conditional associations, not directional effects. Their substantive interpretation is covered in the Gaussian graphical models article.

What does the default figure show?

plot() displays the fitted network using cograph::splot(). Each node represents a construct and each edge an estimated partial correlation. Edge colour distinguishes positive from negative associations, while width indicates their absolute magnitude. Thus, a thicker line signals a larger estimated association, irrespective of its sign.

plot(fit)

The learning-related constructs are connected by several comparatively wide, positive edges. By contrast, the negative edge linking self-regulation and test anxiety is readily distinguishable. The figure provides an overview, but individual edge values should be checked against the estimates. Calling cograph::splot() directly produces the same display and permits the adjustments introduced below.

cograph::splot(fit)

Where should the nodes be placed?

The layout argument controls node placement. A circular layout arranges nodes around a ring, making their positions consistent when the same nodes are supplied in the same order. A spring layout positions more strongly connected nodes nearer to one another, which can make patterns of association easier to see. The seed argument fixes the random starting conditions so that a spring-layout figure can be reproduced.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
cograph::splot(fit, layout = "circle", title = "circle")
cograph::splot(fit, layout = "spring", seed = 11, title = "spring")

par(op)

In the spring layout, cognitive strategy use, self-regulation and intrinsic value appear close together because of their relatively strong connections. Test anxiety lies towards the edge of the diagram, with its negative link to self-regulation particularly evident. This spatial arrangement is generated by the plotting algorithm and is not an additional statistical result. The circular layout is useful for consistent comparisons; the spring layout is useful when exploring the structure of a single network.

How can nodes carry information?

Node size can encode a summary of a construct’s connections. scale_nodes_by = "strength" requests scaling by the network’s strength measure, while node_size_range specifies the range of displayed sizes. The fill, border and label arguments can be adjusted to distinguish nodes and improve legibility. Readers should be told what the size represents, since different centrality measures answer different questions.

cograph::splot(
  fit,
  layout = "circle",
  scale_nodes_by = "strength",
  node_size_range = c(4, 12),
  node_fill = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#CC79A7"),
  node_border_color = "white",
  node_border_width = 2,
  label_size = 0.9,
  title = "Node size scaled by strength"
)

For this signed network, cograph bases the plotted sizes on signed edge weights. The resulting ordering corresponds to expected influence from net_centralities(), rather than to absolute strength. Cognitive strategy use (1.198) and intrinsic value (1.001) have the largest signed values, whereas test anxiety (-0.091) has the smallest. Self-regulation has the highest absolute strength (1.231), but its negative association with test anxiety offsets some of its positive associations, giving an expected influence of 0.532 and a less prominent node. A caption describing nodes as “size by strength” should specify whether signed or absolute weights were used.

How should edges be encoded?

For a signed network, both the direction and magnitude of associations need to be apparent. edge_positive_color and edge_negative_color select colours for the two signs, and edge_width_range maps absolute edge weights to line widths. The threshold argument suppresses edges whose absolute weights fall below a specified value, while edge_labels adds the numerical estimates. Labels are particularly helpful when figures are viewed without colour.

cograph::splot(
  fit,
  layout = "circle",
  threshold = 0.05,
  edge_width_range = c(0.5, 5),
  edge_positive_color = "#0072B2",
  edge_negative_color = "#D55E00",
  edge_labels = TRUE,
  edge_label_size = 0.7,
  edge_label_bg = "white",
  title = "Thresholded edge weights"
)

Here, a threshold of 0.05 conceals the smallest edge, between cognitive strategy use and test anxiety (0.049), leaving nine visible edges with their partial correlations labelled. This is a display decision: the estimated network still contains all 10 edges. Researchers should report the threshold in the caption so that readers do not mistake an omitted line for an estimated zero.

cograph::plot_edge_weights() presents the distribution of estimated edge weights independently of node placement. This view helps distinguish the numerical distribution from the visual prominence of edges in a diagram.

cograph::plot_edge_weights(fit)

The histogram includes one negative edge (-0.350), four positive edges below 0.2 and five stronger positive edges among the learning constructs, with weights reaching 0.412. Three of the four smaller positive edges involve test anxiety. The mean signed edge weight is approximately 0.17. Inspecting this distribution helps assess how a proposed display threshold would affect the information retained in the figure.

How precise are the edges?

A network diagram displays estimated associations, but does not by itself show their precision. net_boot() calculates edge estimates across bootstrap resamples, and plot() displays their intervals. For speed, this illustration uses 250 resamples and the partial-correlation estimator, which is not identical to the regularised estimator used for the original network. For an applied analysis, it is preferable to bootstrap the chosen estimation method and use at least 1,000 resamples. Further guidance appears in the network reliability article.

set.seed(1)
bs <- net_boot(SRL_GPT, method = "pcor", n_boot = 250, cores = 1)
bs
#> <psychnet_bootstrap> pcor, 250 resamples, 95% CI
#>   10 edges (9 significant), 5 nodes, measures: strength, expected_influence
plot(bs)

In this bootstrap output, nine of the 10 edges have 95% intervals that exclude zero. The remaining edge joins cognitive strategy use and test anxiety, consistent with its small point estimate and its omission from the thresholded display. These intervals concern the bootstrap estimator used here. With type = "edge_diff", the plot summarises pairwise comparisons between estimated edge weights:

plot(bs, type = "edge_diff")

difference_test() also provides pairwise edge comparisons and their confidence intervals in tabular form. With style = "forest", the estimated differences and intervals are shown as a forest plot, making their magnitude and uncertainty easier to inspect.

plot(difference_test(bs, type = "edge"), style = "forest")

The output identifies 26 of the 45 edge pairs as differing in size. The forest plot complements the comparison matrix by showing the estimated magnitude and interval of each pairwise difference.

How can a figure follow a house style?

The theme argument provides predefined colour and graphical settings, allowing figures to follow a consistent presentation style without changing the estimated network. The examples below contrast a restrained appearance with a palette designed for colour accessibility.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
cograph::splot(fit, theme = "minimal", title = "minimal")
cograph::splot(fit, theme = "colorblind", title = "colorblind")

par(op)

The colourblind theme is designed to make edge colours easier to distinguish for readers with common forms of colour-vision deficiency. Because colour alone should not carry the interpretation, adding numerical edge labels provides a second way of identifying the sign of an association.

How can networks of several groups be compared?

psychnet() can estimate separate networks for categories identified by group. Here the two model-generated response datasets are combined, and a source indicator identifies the responses from each model. This permits a side-by-side illustration of networks with the same five constructs.

grouped_srl <- rbind(
  data.frame(SRL_GPT, source = "GPT", check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(SRL_Claude, source = "Claude", check.names = FALSE)
)
group_fit <- psychnet(grouped_srl, group = "source", method = "glasso")
summary(group_fit)
#>    group nodes edges mean_abs_weight
#> 1    GPT     5    10       0.2444301
#> 2 Claude     5    10       0.3536997
cograph::splot(group_fit, layout = "circle", psych_styling = TRUE)

cograph::splot() presents the two networks in a grid with a common circular layout. Nodes therefore occupy corresponding positions, making individual connections easier to compare without confounding changes in position with changes in estimated weights. Both networks have 10 edges. The mean absolute edge weight is 0.354 for Claude and 0.244 for GPT, as shown by the group summaries. In the Claude network, intrinsic value and self-efficacy have a negative association; test anxiety is positively associated with cognitive strategy use and negatively associated with self-efficacy. These are descriptive comparisons. Establishing whether between-group differences exceed sampling variation requires a formal comparison using net_compare().

How is the figure saved?

The filename, width, height and res arguments specify the output file and its dimensions and resolution. Export settings should be selected with the intended publication format in mind, with particular attention to whether node labels and edge information remain legible at the final size.

cograph::splot(fit, layout = "circle", filename = "network.png",
               width = 8, height = 8, res = 300)

Summary of the arguments

Task Arguments
Layout layout, seed, layout_scale, layout_margin
Nodes node_size, scale_nodes_by, node_size_range, node_fill, node_shape
Labels labels, label_size, label_color, label_position
Edges edge_width_range, edge_positive_color, edge_negative_color, edge_alpha
Filtering threshold, minimum, maximum
Edge labels edge_labels, edge_label_size, edge_label_bg, edge_label_style
Themes theme, background, title
Export filename, width, height, res

A clear network figure complements, rather than replaces, the estimated edge table and measures of uncertainty. Consistent layouts support comparisons between groups, while explicit node and edge encodings help readers distinguish the results of the analysis from decisions made for visual presentation.
